newsitem.title: CHINA: China prepares for funeral of the decade.
newsitem.headline: China prepares for funeral of the decade.

text.p: China on Sunday prepared for the funeral of the decade, when it pays final respects to departed patriarch Deng Xiaoping while keeping a nervous watch for discord during its delicate period of transition.
Sunday morning dawned crisp and clear in the capital Beijing, with a heightened police presence at centres of power and political sensitivity a reminder that this was no ordinary day of rest.

The security net was particularly conspicuous in the western part of the city at Babaoshan cemetery, where Deng's remains are due to be cremated on Monday prior to memorial rites in Beijing's Great Hall of the People attended by 10,000 people the next day.
A rehearsal for the event on Saturday included a bizarre touch -- a soldier lying inside a glass casket, apparently simulating China's late paramount leader.
At around midnight on Saturday, the capital's vast Tiananmen Square was deserted save for police manning every street and subway entrance.
Tiananmen has a particular resonance for Chinese: it was the site of the single most infamous event of the Deng era when he sanctioned troops and tanks to crush pro-democracy demonstrations in 1989.

Deng, dubbed the architect of modern China for his fundamental economic reforms, died on Wednesday at the age of 92. In accordance with his wishes, his body will be cremated and his ashes will be scattered at sea.
While the funeral ceremony itself is certain to feature careful expressions of grief by top leaders, Beijing has taken pains to ensure that no unexpected expressions of popular sorrow take place.
Several citizens who attempted to place floral tributes to Deng at Tiananmen Square on Thursday were hustled away by police.
Apart from tightening security, China's leadership under Deng's protege President Jiang Zemin has striven to present an image of business as usual.
Jiang has already pledged not to swerve from the judicious mix of market reform and communist control that was the trademark of the 18-year-long Deng era.
He vowed to outdo the achievements of the man whose vision launched the fastest economic boom the world has even seen and transformed a lumbering Stalinist giant into a fledgling superpower.
China's powerful military issued a promise of allegiance to Deng's successor, its commander Jiang, vowing to "rally closely" around his leadership.

The support of the three-million-strong People's Liberation Army is essential to Jiang, who also holds the posts of Communist Party chief and head of the armed forces, and a show of allegiance was expected when China's leadership wants to present a united front.

Emphasising that government functions have not been paralysed by the death of Deng, the Xinhua news agency announced late on Saturday that the new mayor of Beijing, Jia Qinglin, had been formally elected.
Jia pledged allegiance to Jiang, his mentor.

China is also keeping the foreign policy wheels turning. New U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrives on Monday as scheduled, although her visit has been shortened in deference to the funeral rites for Deng.
